topic: How HTTPS keeps your data private
scope_note: Mechanism and promises of HTTPS for non-technical employees: plain HTTP exposure, handshake, certificate check, shared session key, encrypted and integrity-protected traffic, and what the padlock does and does not mean. No versions, algorithms, key lengths, statistics or dates.

facts.statement: With plain HTTP, the data travels unprotected, so anyone who can see the traffic on its path can read it.
On a shared network such as public wifi, other devices and the network operator may be positioned where they can see traffic passing along the path.
facts.caveat: Say 'may be able to'; this describes possibility, not that a given network is being watched.

facts.statement: HTTPS is ordinary HTTP carried inside a protected connection created by TLS (Transport Layer Security).
Before any application data such as a login is sent, the browser and the server run a short exchange called the TLS handshake.
During the handshake the server presents a digital certificate that ties its name to its public key, to prove who it is.
A certificate is issued by a certificate authority, an organisation that browsers and operating systems already trust.
The browser checks that the certificate was issued by a trusted authority, that the name on it matches the address being visited, and that today's date falls within its validity dates.
facts.caveat: Browsers perform further checks (for example revocation); the lesson names only these three.

facts.statement: If the certificate fails a check (wrong name, expired, or untrusted issuer), the browser shows a warning instead of silently continuing.
facts.caveat: Wording and the option to proceed vary by browser; say 'warns', not 'always blocks'.

facts.statement: The browser and server use key exchange to agree a shared secret session key without ever sending that key readable across the network.
facts.caveat: State the idea and result only, not the mathematics.
facts.reference_hint: Diffie-Hellman key exchange (public-key cryptography); used in TLS

facts.statement: An eavesdropper who records every message of the key exchange still cannot work out the session key.
facts.caveat: Holds for a passive watcher when the exchange is correctly implemented with current methods; the lesson should say 'cannot realistically work out', and the identity check in F7 is what stops an active impostor.

facts.statement: After the handshake, the data in both directions is encrypted with the shared session key, using symmetric encryption where both ends use the same key.
Encrypted data looks like meaningless noise to a watcher, and only the two ends holding the session key can turn it back into readable data.
TLS also protects integrity: if data is altered in transit, the receiving end detects the change.
facts.caveat: Detection, not prevention: someone on the path can still disrupt or drop traffic, but cannot change it unnoticed.

facts.statement: HTTPS therefore provides three things: confidentiality (others cannot read the data), integrity (changes are detected) and authentication of the server (you are talking to the named site).
The browser's padlock means the connection is private and is with the site named in the address bar.
facts.caveat: Browsers have changed how the padlock looks and is labelled; speak of the idea, not the exact icon.

facts.statement: The padlock does not mean the site is honest, safe, or free of phishing or malware, because a site run by a bad actor can also obtain a valid certificate for its own name.
HTTPS does not hide which site you connect to: a watcher on the path can still tell which server the traffic is going to.
facts.caveat: Which host is visible, and by which means, varies with newer privacy features; say 'does not reliably hide', and that the content of the visit is what is protected.

facts.statement: HTTPS protects data only while it travels; once it reaches the server, the server can read it and what it does with it is up to the site.

terms.definition: The short opening exchange in which browser and server check identity and agree a session key before any data is sent.
A digital document that ties a site's name to its public key, issued by a certificate authority.
An organisation that browsers already trust to issue certificates.
The shared secret both ends use to scramble and unscramble data for this one connection.
Scrambling data so that only someone with the right key can read it.
The assurance that data was not changed on the way, or that a change is detected.

not_claimed: The padlock means the site is safe, honest or trustworthy.
HTTPS protects against phishing or malware.
HTTPS hides which site you are visiting.
HTTPS protects data once it reaches the server or after it is stored there.
The session key is sent to the server in a form a watcher could read.
Any statistic about HTTPS adoption, or any dates, versions, algorithm names or key lengths.
Public wifi is always being watched, or HTTPS makes public wifi risk-free in every respect.
